newsitem.title: THAILAND: Bangkok Bank of Commerce's future hazy.
newsitem.headline: Bangkok Bank of Commerce's future hazy.

text.p: Ailing Bangkok Bank of Commerce's future looks gloomy given its huge debts, but analysts see rays of hope provided a Thai central bank rescue plan is handled well.

"Bangkok Bank of Commerce's bad loan problem is quite serious. However the central bank is making full efforts to turn it around to prove its credibility," said Thanadech Mahapokai, an analyst at Book Club Finance and Securities.
Last week, the bank said it was saddled with net non-performing loans, after collateral deduction, of 53.78 billion baht ($2.07 billion) at end-1996.
The bank's outstanding loans and interest receivables stood at 87.1 billion baht at end-1996 against 64.4 billion baht in 1995.
It posted a huge 24.8 billion baht net loss in 1996 against an 860.4 million profit in 1995.
Under the central bank's rescue plan, the semi-state-owned Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand will be allowed an 18 percent stake in the bank and will manage it for seven years.
Bank of Thailand governor Rerngchai Marakanond said on Friday that IFCT nominees were expected to start running the bank from May 1.
This would be after a bank shareholders meeting on April 30 to approve the new management team and plans proposed by IFCT and the central bank.

"There is no doubt about the IFCT's ability to manage Bangkok Bank of Commerce. IFCT has already proved their capability to manage an ailing financial institution like First City Investment," said Thanadech.
IFCT was asked by the government in 1993 to bail out First City Investment Plc which was on the verge of collapse and unable to honour its debts.
Bangkok Bank of Commerce shares lost over 75 percent of their value on Thursday when trading was resumed after an 11-month suspension to consider a possible delisting.
But on Friday the share price rose the daily 10 percent limit to four baht.
The bourse said the stock would be suspended again on May 19 after a month of trading and a decision made on its future.

"Whether the price of the bank's stocks would rise quickly or not depends entirely on the duration of the bailout plan and the level of its success," said a broker. "You can make a huge profit but only on a long-term investment basis."
Other analysts said the delisting of the bank shares appeared unlikely because there was some confidence that the central bank and the IFCT could return the bank to profitability.
"The key concern now is how long IFCT will take to turn around the bank. It's doubtful, and bad loans are very large," said Thanita Leelahawan, banking analyst at Multi-Credit Corp of Thailand.

However, Rerngchai said the bank may post a profit this year as it had been told to raise provisioning for non-performing loans and it had written off about 27 billion baht of its total bad loans last year.
